question: Tell us about a self-supervised or foundation model you have worked with, whether trained from scratch, pretrained, or adapted to a downstream task. What did you do with it, and how did you evaluate whether it worked well for your use case?
answer: I worked with frozen BioCLIP and DINOv3 visual representations for plant identification at Arborphy AI. I adapted BioCLIP into an EfficientNet–BioCLIP dual-encoder with bidirectional spatial cross-attention, auxiliary organ supervision, and BioCLIP-anchored gated residuals to test whether biological semantic features and CNN image features were complementary. I evaluated it with controlled fusion experiments against single encoders, concatenation, and one-way versus two-way cross-attention, using individual-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out evaluations. The fusion macro-F1 improved from 0.808 to 0.832 across iterations, but the more important finding was that the gains were not reliable over BioCLIP alone. I also used frozen linear probes, clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, and cross-species retrieval benchmarks to separate species identity, organ morphology, and photographic-scale confounding. That kind of rigorous downstream evaluation maps well to Artera’s whole-slide outcome and molecular-trait modeling.

question: Describe a project where your model did not generalize as well as expected across datasets, sites, devices, populations, or other conditions. How did you investigate the problem, and what did you try to improve robustness?
answer: In my plant-identification work at Arborphy, I built an EfficientNet–BioCLIP dual-encoder fusion model that initially looked stronger through architecture iterations, but did not generalize into a reliable species-recognition improvement over BioCLIP alone under stricter evaluation. I investigated it by separating representation questions from model-capacity questions: frozen linear probes, multi-seed clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, local PCA rotations, and centroid shrinkage helped me distinguish species identity from organ morphology and photographic-scale confounding. I also ran controlled comparisons of single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional cross-attention with individual-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out evaluations. To improve robustness, I tried bidirectional spatial cross-attention, auxiliary organ supervision, and BioCLIP-anchored gated residuals to reduce negative transfer. The main lesson I would bring to Artera is not to trust a better aggregate score until it survives grouped, disjoint evaluation.

question: Describe a clinical, biological, or other real-world problem you helped translate into a machine-learning problem. How did you define the prediction target and decide how to evaluate the model?
answer: At Arborphy, I worked on plant identification as a biological recognition problem: given plant imagery, could a model distinguish species identity without simply learning organ type, individual plant appearance, or photographic scale. I defined the main prediction target as species recognition, and used organ information as auxiliary supervision to test whether morphology helped or caused negative transfer. For evaluation, I focused on whether the model held up under stricter splits, not just whether a fused architecture looked better once. I compared single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional cross-attention, then used individual-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out evaluations. That changed the conclusion: although fusion macro-F1 improved across iterations, the controlled evaluations found no reliable species-recognition advantage over BioCLIP alone. That is the kind of target/evaluation discipline I would bring to patient-outcome or molecular-trait modeling at Artera.
